books.section: Topic 6.12 Controversies over the Role of Government in the Gilded Age
The Silver Issue and the Populist Movement

primary_sources: Frederick Burr Opper, 'The Silver-Tongued Ventriloquist and His Dummies,' Puck, August 12, 1896

stimulus.text: Political cartoon, “The Silver-Tongued Ventriloquist and His Dummies,” by Frederick Burr Opper, Puck, August 12, 1896. A large bearded man wearing a sash labeled “Silver Mine Owner” sits on a box marked “16 to 1.” He holds a small dummy labeled “Bryan” who waves a paper reading “Free Silver Harangues.” At the left, three more small dummies sit in a box, labeled “Tillman,” “Peffer,” and “Altgeld.” At the right, another dummy labeled “Sewall” sits in a box. The caption reads, “If the Show Succeeds, He’ll Get All the Profits.”
stimulus.source_note: Frederick Burr Opper, 'The Silver-Tongued Ventriloquist and His Dummies,' Puck, August 12, 1896. Public domain: cartoon published 1896 (pre-1930); Library of Congress, LCCN2012648552. Labels and caption checked against the image.

stem: What does “16 to 1” on the box refer to?

options.text: The number of states Bryan carried in 1896
options.misconception: Bryan carried 22 states in 1896, and '16 to 1' was the silver coinage ratio.

options.text: The price of an ounce of silver in dollars
options.misconception: '16 to 1' was a ratio of silver to gold, not a price in dollars.

options.text: The year in which the cartoon was published
options.misconception: The cartoon was published in 1896, and '16 to 1' was the silver coinage ratio.

options.text: The ratio for coining silver and gold under free silver

rationales.A: Bryan carried 22 states, and 16 to 1 was the coinage ratio.
rationales.B: 16 to 1 was a ratio of silver to gold, not a price.
rationales.C: The cartoon was published in 1896, and 16 to 1 was the coinage ratio.
rationales.D: Free silver meant coining silver and gold at the legal ratio of 16 to 1.
rationales.general:
Read the number with the debate.
1. The box marked '16 to 1' is the seat of the silver mine owner.
2. The dummy waves a paper reading 'Free Silver Harangues.'
3. Background from the books: free silver meant coining silver and gold at 16 to 1.
4. The number is the heart of the silver plan, not a count of states or a price.
Remember: a number in a cartoon usually names the policy, so ask which policy it fits.
